days.title: A Candidate Talked So Long I Zoned Out
days.text:
A teacher candidate talked so long, I zoned out. In my own interview. 😵

I asked her a question she clearly didn't know how to answer. So she just started talking. And talking.

When she finally stopped, my colleague had to prompt me to ask the next question.

Swipe for why it happens, and the 3-step answer that keeps you from ever doing it. 👉

Principals and hiring committees: what's the longest answer you've ever sat through? 👇

More stories from my years of hiring teachers are in my book Professional Interview Secrets. Link in bio.

days.title: A Smartboard Is a Glorified Chalkboard
days.text:
40 of my last 60 teacher candidates told me the same thing about technology: "We have a smartboard." 🖥️

days.title: A Student Is Yelling. Phones Are Out. What Do You Do?
days.text:
School leaders: A, B, C or D? 📱

A student starts yelling in the hallway. Phones come out. Staff are watching.

A. Issue a firm public command immediately.
B. Lower your voice, reduce crowd stimulus, then set a boundary.
C. Pull the student aside before naming the boundary.
D. Hand off to security and step back.

Comment your letter. 👇

This is from Regulation Under Pressure, a free module in my H.E.L.P. course for school leaders. Pressure changes your pace before it changes your words. Link in bio.

days.label: What would you do? Scenario 08, The Vendor Table (carousel; video on YouTube)
days.title: Principals: What Would You Do? The Vendor Table
days.text:
Principals and teachers: what would you do? 🤔

The PTA president asks if her friend can sell merchandise at the school carnival fundraiser. Private sales aren't allowed. The superintendent confirms it. You say no.

Carnival day: the friend shows up with a table anyway. She says the PTA president told her, "He will not even realize you are here."

The person who should protect the boundary went around it. What's your move? Comment your call. What I chose is in the first comment.

This is one of 12 real scenarios in my What Would You Do? 12 School Leadership Scenarios deck, where you make the call before you see how I handled it. Link in bio.

#principallife #schoolleadership #pta #whatwouldyoudo #assistantprincipal #teachertok
days.first_comment:
What I chose: I asked the vendor to leave. At the next PTA meeting I told the president plainly that going behind my back had damaged my confidence in our partnership. The larger PTA board learned what happened and asked her to step down. That was the group's decision, not mine.

Trust is built when people know the rules apply even to those with influence.

linkedin.text:
I once had a teacher candidate who, when I asked a question she clearly didn't know how to answer, just began talking. And talking.

It was so bad that when she finally stopped, my colleague had to prompt me to ask the next question. I had completely zoned out.

Word vomit usually happens when you don't know the answer. You start fishing, throwing everything out there in hopes that something satisfies the question.

Stories and details belong in a good interview. The problem is going off topic and never wrapping up.

The safe formula: answer the question, relate it to an experience from your classroom, and conclude. And read the room. If your interviewer is glazing over, you may be in the middle of a word vomit.

Principals: what's the longest answer you've ever sat through?

#TeacherInterview #Education #Hiring #K12

linkedin.text:
Of the last 60 teacher interviews I conducted, I would safely say at least 40 candidates told me they had a smartboard.

Let's be clear. A smartboard is nothing but a glorified chalkboard unless you're taking advantage of its many interactive features.

Same with apps and websites. Showing your students a video doesn't equal implementing technology in your classroom. It's no different than when teachers showed film strips years ago.

What I want to hear instead: the technology that's been a game changer in your classroom. The site or app you infused into a lesson to create a unique, innovative experience for your students.

And be ready for the real questions. How did it increase your students' digital age skills? How are your students being creative with it?

If you don't have that experience yet, it's time to go get some.

School leaders: what do you listen for when a candidate talks about technology?

poll.question: A student is yelling in the hallway. Phones are out and staff are watching. What's your first move?

linkedin.text:
Pressure changes your pace before it changes your words.

A student starts yelling in the hallway. Phones come out. Staff are watching.

In that moment, pressure tempts a leader to match the volume to prove control.

But authority and volume are two different things. A quieter voice can become the strongest authority signal in a loud space.

School leaders: what's your first move?

linkedin.cta: Books (From City Streets to The Classroom)
linkedin.text:
There's a stereotype about teaching jobs in city schools: "I couldn't get a job in a good school, so this is my second choice."

In my book From City Streets to The Classroom, I wrote that educators and administrators must not let that notion infiltrate their minds. If we view these jobs as temporary until something better comes along, we perpetuate the stereotype.

The kids notice. When I started as the music teacher in a Pittsburgh city middle school, students told me, "You'll never last." They had watched too many adults leave.

The kids in city schools need great teachers more than anyone. We should expect nothing but the highest quality teachers, because our kids need it.

Principals: how do you keep great teachers in the buildings that need them most?

#UrbanEducation #SchoolLeadership #TeacherRetention #Education
